title: Paediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock: Recognition and Emergency Management

evidenceAudit.scope: Children and young people under 16 years with suspected sepsis or septic shock in emergency, ward and paediatric assessment settings: age-banded risk stratification, the first-hour bundle, empirical antibiotics by age, fluid bolus rules, oxygen, source finding and escalation to paediatric critical care.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-22.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi Ministry of Health paediatric sepsis protocol was located in this session; hospital antimicrobial policy and the Saudi paediatric early warning tool in use locally take precedence.
Benzylpenicillin and gentamicin doses for babies within 72 hours of birth (NICE recommendation 1.8.5) were not stated in the opened text and are not given here; use the neonatal unit protocol.
Cefotaxime was checked against NICE recommendation 1.8.6 only; its product label was not opened.
No sourced penicillin-allergy alternative was found in NICE NG254 or the Surviving Sepsis Campaign (SSC) page; discuss severe beta-lactam allergy with paediatric infectious diseases or microbiology.
Vasoactive doses (adrenaline, noradrenaline) were not opened; the SSC 2026 page states no preferred agent, and dosing belongs to paediatric critical care.
The ampicillin label was read from a third-party reproduction (PrescriberPoint), not DailyMed; its renal dosing section was not shown.
Table 3 of NICE NG254 (ages 12 to 15) was not opened; use adult-style criteria from that table locally.
SFDA: the Saudi Food and Drug Authority register could not be opened from this environment, so registration of this product in Saudi Arabia was not verified; check the register before prescribing.

pathophysiology.summary: Sepsis is a dysregulated host response to infection that produces organ dysfunction; in children circulatory failure often presents first as tachycardia and prolonged capillary refill while blood pressure is still maintained. Rising lactate reflects tissue hypoperfusion; NICE NG254 uses venous lactate over 2 mmol/litre to upgrade moderate risk and over 4 mmol/litre to trigger an immediate fluid bolus and critical care referral. Hypotension is a late sign in younger children, so NICE uses blood pressure as a bolus trigger only from age 12 (systolic 90 mmHg or less). Neonates and young infants have immature immunity and acquire organisms from the maternal genital tract (group B streptococcus, Escherichia coli, listeria), which is why empirical cover changes below 3 months. Fluid overload is harmful where critical care is not available: the SSC 2026 guideline recommends against bolus fluid in children without hypotension in such settings.

symptoms: Parent or carer concern that the child is behaving differently from usual.
Fever, or temperature below 36 °C at any age.
Drowsiness, reduced feeding, weak or continuous high-pitched cry in infants.
Leg pain and cold hands or feet.
Reduced urine output or fewer wet nappies.
Symptoms pointing to a source: cough, vomiting, dysuria, rash, painful joint or headache.
physicalSigns: Tachycardia above the NICE age-band threshold, or bradycardia below 60 beats per minute.
Tachypnoea above the age-band threshold; grunting, nasal flaring or apnoea.
Capillary refill time of 3 seconds or more; mottled or ashen skin.
Oxygen saturation below 92% (moderate to high risk) or below 90% (high risk) in air.
Altered mental state: does not wake, or if roused does not stay awake.
redFlags: Any NICE high risk criterion (Table 1 under 5s, Table 2 ages 5 to 11): start the first-hour bundle.
Temperature 38 °C or more in a baby under 3 months.
Non-blanching rash with fever: treat as possible meningococcal sepsis.
No response within 1 hour of any intervention: a consultant attends in person (NICE recommendation 1.7.11).
No improvement after two fluid boluses.
precipitants: Recent surgery, indwelling lines or devices.
Skin breach: burns, varicella lesions, wounds.
Pneumonia, urinary tract infection, meningitis and intra-abdominal infection as the commonest sources.

differentials.condition: Viral infection with fever and tachycardia
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Child appears well between fever spikes, normal capillary refill, normal lactate and improving heart rate with antipyretic; still reassess against NICE tables hourly.
High blood glucose with ketones and metabolic acidosis on blood gas; deep sighing respiration rather than shock as the main feature; fluid rules differ.
Clear losses from diarrhoea and vomiting with rapid response to fluid; sepsis remains possible if the child is febrile and unwell.

differentials.condition: Congenital heart disease or cardiomyopathy presenting with shock
differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Hepatomegaly, gallop rhythm, murmur, cardiomegaly on chest X-ray, worsening with fluid boluses; seek cardiology input early.
History inconsistent with findings, bruising patterns, unexplained drowsiness; follow safeguarding procedures alongside resuscitation.

ruleIn.testName: Venous blood gas with lactate and glucose
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Lactate over 2 mmol/litre upgrades moderate risk to high risk; over 4 mmol/litre triggers a fluid bolus and critical care referral.
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Take with the first venous sample (NICE recommendation 1.7.2); the SSC 2026 guideline also recommends lactate in initial evaluation. Repeat after each bolus.

references.edition: NICE NG254 (2024 update), Section Managing suspected sepsis, Recommendations 1.7.2–1.7.19

clinicalManagement.title: Recognise and grade risk
actions: Think sepsis in any unwell child with signs of infection.
Grade risk against NICE NG254 Table 1 (under 5) or Table 2 (5 to 11) using behaviour, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, capillary refill, skin and temperature.
Take parent or carer concern seriously; it is a moderate to high risk criterion.
Record the time a high risk criterion was first met: the 1-hour clock starts there.

clinicalManagement.title: High risk: first-hour bundle
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 hour of meeting any high risk criterion
actions: Senior clinical decision maker assesses urgently; discuss with a consultant (recommendation 1.7.2).
Venous blood gas with glucose and lactate, blood culture, full blood count, kidney function.
Give the age-appropriate broad-spectrum antibiotic without delay (recommendations 1.8.5–1.8.8).
Give oxygen if signs of shock or oxygen saturation below 92% in air.
Monitor continuously, or at least every 30 minutes, including mental state.

clinicalManagement.title: Fluid bolus and critical care referral
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Within 1 hour, when lactate over 4 mmol/litre (or systolic 90 mmHg or less at ages 12–15)
actions: Give 10 mL/kg glucose-free crystalloid with sodium 130–154 mmol/litre over less than 10 minutes, maximum 250 mL; use a pump or syringe under 12.
Reassess after each bolus; if no improvement give a second bolus.
If still no improvement after the second bolus, a consultant attends in person.
Refer to paediatric critical care; where critical care is not available and the child is not hypotensive, avoid bolus fluid and start maintenance fluid (SSC 2026).
Vasoactive medicine may be started through a peripheral vein rather than delayed (SSC 2026); dosing by critical care.

clinicalManagement.title: Moderate to high risk pathway
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Clinician review within 1 hour; senior review within 3 hours
actions: With two or more criteria: blood gas with lactate and clinician review of results within 1 hour.
Lactate over 2 mmol/litre (or acute kidney injury at ages 12–15): manage as high risk.
Lactate 2 mmol/litre or less with no definitive diagnosis: repeat structured assessment at least hourly and senior review of the need for antibiotics within 3 hours.
One criterion only: clinician review within 1 hour and blood tests if indicated.

clinicalManagement.title: Find and control the source
actions: Tailor tests to history and examination; consider urinalysis and chest X-ray in all.
Lumbar puncture in babies under 1 month and in qualifying babies 1–3 months, unless contraindicated; never delay antibiotics for it.
Image abdomen and pelvis if no source is found.
Involve the surgical or interventional radiology team early when drainage or surgery is suitable.

clinicalManagement.title: Ongoing care and de-escalation
actions: Narrow antibiotics once the organism and sensitivities are known (SSC 2026).
Do not give routine hydrocortisone if haemodynamically stable after fluids and vasoactive therapy; give stress-dose steroid for suspected or documented adrenal insufficiency.
Do not give routine intravenous immunoglobulin or vitamin C.
Follow hospital antimicrobial policy for hospital-acquired sepsis (recommendation 1.8.9).
Notify suspected meningococcal disease to public health per local rules.

regimens.indication: Fluid resuscitation in suspected sepsis meeting bolus criteria
regimens.frequency: Over less than 10 minutes; reassess after each bolus
regimens.duration: Second bolus if no improvement; consultant in person if no improvement after the second; the SSC 2026 guideline suggests up to 40–60 mL/kg in the first hour only where critical care is available
adjustments: Smaller volumes may be needed with heart failure or kidney failure (NICE recommendation 1.9.2).

monitoring: Heart rate, capillary refill, mental state and lactate after each bolus.
Signs of fluid overload: crackles, hepatomegaly, rising oxygen requirement.
contraindications: Signs of fluid overload or cardiogenic shock.
Glucose-containing fluids must not be used for bolus.

medicationPlan.note: Empirical antibiotics follow NICE NG254 by age. Babies presenting in hospital within 72 hours of birth receive intravenous benzylpenicillin with gentamicin (recommendation 1.8.5) dosed by the neonatal unit protocol; children already in hospital follow the local hospital-acquired infection policy (recommendation 1.8.9). Penicillin allergy: no alternative is given in the sources opened; ceftriaxone is used cautiously in penicillin-sensitive children and a history of severe beta-lactam reaction needs paediatric infectious diseases or microbiology advice before the first dose is delayed. Vasoactive and corticosteroid dosing sits with paediatric critical care.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Signs or symptoms of infection in a child who appears unwell, with risk then graded against NICE NG254 Tables 1 and 2.

Any one of: no response to social cues; appears ill to a healthcare professional; respiratory rate 60 or more (under 1 year), 50 or more (1–2 years), 40 or more (3–4 years); heart rate 160 or more (under 1 year), 150 or more (1–2 years), 140 or more (3–4 years), or below 60; capillary refill 3 seconds or more; oxygen saturation below 90% in air; mottled skin; non-blanching rash.

Any one of: altered behaviour or mental state; respiratory rate 29 or more (age 5), 27 or more (6–7), 25 or more (8–11); heart rate 130 or more (5), 120 or more (6–7), 115 or more (8–11), or below 60; capillary refill 3 seconds or more; oxygen saturation below 90% in air.

Two or more moderate to high risk criteria (for example oxygen saturation below 92% in air, decreased activity, cold hands or feet, leg pain, heart or respiratory rate in the moderate band) prompts blood gas with lactate and clinician review within 1 hour.

diagnosticCriteria.criterion: Septic shock (working definition for this pathway)
diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Suspected sepsis with signs of circulatory failure (capillary refill 3 seconds or more, mottling, reduced urine output, lactate over 4 mmol/litre, or hypotension) persisting after fluid boluses, needing vasoactive support.

guidelineComparison.note: This pathway follows NICE for antibiotic choice and bolus size and adds the SSC 2026 limits on fluid where critical care is unavailable. The label threshold of 41 weeks is the stricter neonatal ceftriaxone limit and is flagged in the regimen.

teaching.scope: Children and young people under 16 years with suspected sepsis or septic shock in emergency, ward and paediatric assessment settings: age-banded risk stratification, the first-hour bundle, empirical antibiotics by age, fluid bolus rules, oxygen, source finding and escalation to paediatric critical care.
learningObjectives: Grade risk in an unwell child with infection using the NICE NG254 age-banded tables.
Deliver antibiotics, blood gas with lactate and blood culture within 1 hour of a high risk criterion.
Choose empirical antibiotics by age, including listeria cover below 3 months.
Give and reassess 10 mL/kg crystalloid boluses and know when fluid is harmful.
Escalate to a consultant and paediatric critical care at the right triggers.
pitfalls: Waiting for hypotension before treating shock in a young child.
Giving glucose-containing fluid as a bolus.
Repeating boluses without reassessment, or in a setting without critical care when the child is not hypotensive.
Forgetting listeria cover in babies under 3 months.
keyPoints: Tachycardia and capillary refill change before blood pressure in young children.
Lactate over 2 mmol/litre upgrades risk; over 4 mmol/litre means bolus and critical care.
Under 3 months add ampicillin to the cephalosporin for listeria.
Ceftriaxone is avoided in hyperbilirubinaemic or premature neonates and with intravenous calcium.
Do not delay antibiotics for lumbar puncture or imaging.

patientEducation: Explain to parents that sepsis is the body's severe reaction to infection and that early antibiotics and fluids are being given because of specific warning signs.
Tell parents to report at once if the child becomes harder to wake, develops a rash that does not fade under pressure, breathes fast or stops passing urine.
On discharge after low-risk assessment, give written safety-netting advice on when to return.
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep routine childhood immunisations up to date, including pneumococcal, Haemophilus influenzae type b and meningococcal vaccines.
Good hand hygiene and line care for children with indwelling devices.
Maintain fluids and feeding during febrile illness at home.
mdtReferrals: Paediatric critical care or retrieval team for lactate over 4 mmol/litre or failure to respond to two boluses.
Paediatric infectious diseases or microbiology for severe beta-lactam allergy, resistant organisms or hospital-acquired sepsis.
Paediatric surgery or interventional radiology for source control.
Neonatal team for babies under 28 days.
Safeguarding team where the history raises concern.
Paediatric pharmacist for weight-based dosing and renal adjustment.
dischargeCriteria: No high or moderate to high risk criteria on repeated structured assessment.
Source identified and treated, with oral switch agreed by a senior clinician.
Feeding and drinking adequately with normal urine output.
Parents understand warning signs and have written safety-netting advice.
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Review culture results within 48 hours and adjust or stop antibiotics; arrange paediatric follow-up after septic shock or critical care admission to look for physical, cognitive and emotional after-effects; check immunisation status and complete any missed vaccines.
